text: Arthur William Bacot (28 April 1866 – 12 April 1922) was an entomologist at the Lister Institute of Preventive Medicine. Born in North London, he was the third son and fourth child of Edmund Alexander Bacot and Harriet. Bacot was a poor attender at school, leaving at the age of sixteen in 1882, and subsequently worked as an office worker in the City of London. He had no formal scientific training beyond membership in the London Natural History Society. A dedicated butterfly collector, he authored over fifty papers on British lepidoptera between 1893 and 1909. In 1908, he began researching morphological and genetic topics, conducting breeding experiments with the geometrid moth Acidalia virginaria (binomial name Scopula modicaria), which he presented to the London Hospital Medical School. Professor Greenwood of the Advisory Committee for Plague Investigation sought someone to study the breeding habits of the rat flea and its transmission of the plague virus; Bacot was asked to undertake this research in his spare time with a small fee and all expenses covered. The project succeeded, leading to his appointment at the Lister Institute. In 1914, during the First World War, he traveled to Sierra Leone in British West Africa to study Yellow Fever. By autumn 1917, concerns arose about the reduced efficiency of the British Expeditionary Force in France due to trench fever; Bacot, alongside Joseph Arkwright, investigated the disease's cause and prevention, identifying the link between lice and both typhus and trench fever. Bacot contracted trench fever himself while in Warsaw. In 1922, he went to Cairo with Arkwright at the request of the Egyptian Government to study typhus; both contracted the disease from lice. Arkwright survived after a prolonged illness, while Bacot died at the age of 55.
